name: Karl Popper
role: Austrian-British philosopher of science and political thought (1902-1994)
summary: Popper, author of The Open Society and Its Enemies, defended liberal democracy as the system that lets a government be removed without bloodshed, opposed historicism, utopian social engineering and Marxist prophecy, and argued that tolerance must not extend to those who would destroy it.

sources.title: Conjeturas y refutaciones: el desarrollo del conocimiento científico (Paidós, 1983; Spanish translation of Conjectures and Refutations, 1963), Internet Archive full text
sources.author: Karl Popper
sources.usedFor: Democracy as removing a government without bloodshed, utopian engineering and violence, critique of Marx's historical prophecy.

sources.title: Tolerancia y responsabilidad intelectual (Cuadernos de reflexion 3, 1984; Spanish translation of Popper's lecture on toleration), Internet Archive full text
sources.author: Karl Popper
sources.usedFor: Limits of tolerance, relativism and critical pluralism.

sources.title: Popper and the Paradox of Tolerance, Skepchick, 2017 (reproduces the passage from The Open Society and Its Enemies, vol. 1, ch. 7 note 4, in full)
sources.author: Karl Popper, quoted by Skepchick
sources.usedFor: The verbatim paradox-of-tolerance passage from The Open Society.

sources.title: Brian J. Gladish, 'The Society Most Conducive to Problem Solving: Karl Popper and Piecemeal Social Engineering', The Independent Review 24(3), Winter 2019/20
sources.author: Brian J. Gladish
sources.usedFor: Quotes The Open Society on 'unrestrained capitalism', state intervention limited to the protection of freedom, and piecemeal blueprints for health and unemployment insurance.

universal-healthcare.rationale: In 'Utopia and Violence' he said to fight epidemics and disease 'by creating hospitals and schools of medicine', and the Open Society as quoted by Gladish lists 'health and unemployed insurance' among his piecemeal blueprints; in his optimistic lecture he counted what the welfare state achieved against disease and unemployment (translated from the Spanish).

notes: First audit. Popper is a philosopher with a large political output, but his main political books are borrow-only online (see notFound), so the answers rest on two open Spanish translations: Conjeturas y refutaciones (1983), read by theme (democracy, violence, utopian engineering, Marx, historicism, toleration) and the lecture Tolerancia y responsabilidad intelectual (1984). Quotations in the rationales are my translations from the Spanish. The Open Society itself is borrow-only, so its passages are cited through quoting sources (Skepchick for the tolerance note, Gladish for the interventionism passages); the 1988 Economist article on democracy (only a truncated repost and an unresolved short link were reachable) and the 1992 Kyoto lecture were not found as text. Beyond the answers, the liberal theses in 'Public opinion and liberal principles' (the state as a necessary evil whose powers must not be multiplied beyond need, yet the individual needing the state's protection against public opinion; equality before the law; economic equality as a possible threat to freedom) and the passage on free markets and unintended consequences were read and fit no statement closely enough; statements about markets, welfare and the state stay null.
